---
title: "Can we trust the result?"
subtitle: "Publication bias, robustness and sensitivity"
---



## Learning objectives {.objectives}

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

1.  List the ways a set of studies can be a **biased sample** of the evidence.
2.  Read a **contour-enhanced funnel plot** — and explain why asymmetry ≠ publication bias.
3.  Test for small-study effects and time-lag bias **with dependent effect sizes**, and know which classic methods to avoid.
4.  Run **sensitivity analyses** (leave-one-study-out, influence, study quality) and report robustness.

::: notes
60 min: ~20 min slides, ~33 min practical, ~5 min debrief. Much of the conceptual content is adapted, with thanks, from Dakis-Yaoba Ouédraogo's 2024 lecture. Same running example as this afternoon: pests, intercropping vs monoculture, multilevel model (−27%).
:::

## Are our 28 studies a fair sample?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
A meta-analysis assumes the studies it contains are **representative** of all studies done.

But studies with **significant** results are more likely to be:

-   **published** → *publication bias*
-   published **quickly** → *time-lag bias*
-   published **in English** → *language bias*
-   published **more than once** → *multiple-publication bias*
-   **cited** (and found) → *citation bias*
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.fragment .box .warn}
[The consequence]{.box-title}
The pooled effect can be **overestimated** — sometimes an effect appears where there is none.
:::

::: {.fragment .box .green}
[The best cure is prevention]{.box-title}
Search grey literature, theses, reports and non-English studies (Monday's sessions). The tests we see today can only **detect** and **probe** bias — never repair it.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.source}
Adapted from @ouedraogo2024; see also @koricheva2013, chap. 14.
:::

# Publication bias {.section-divider background-image="../../theme/img/bg-keymessages.jpg"}

## The logic of the funnel plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](slides_files/figure-revealjs/plot-funnel-theory-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Large studies (top) cluster near the true effect; small ones (bottom) scatter **symmetrically** → a funnel.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.fragment}
*Where would the missing studies be?*\
Small **non-significant** studies (between the dotted lines) stay in drawers → a corner is **missing**.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Simulated data. Ask the question before revealing the fragment. Dotted lines: ±1.96 SE around ZERO = significance boundaries.
:::

## Our funnel, with significance contours

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](slides_files/figure-revealjs/plot-funnel-ours-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
-   Shaded bands: significance of each comparison (grey background: *p* < 0.01)
-   Dashed line: the multilevel mean
-   Top: 83 comparisons from 2 studies with SE < 0.02 — suspiciously precise: check the extraction

::: {.fragment .box .blue}
If missing studies were in the **white** zone (non-significant), publication bias is a plausible cause. If they would sit in significant zones, look for other causes [@peters2008].
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
~2 min. The bottom of the funnel is roughly symmetric around 0, with imprecise comparisons on both sides, some in the white zone: no obvious gap of non-significant results. The very top (SE < 0.02) comes from 2 studies (525, 645) — possibly SEs entered as SDs, and study 525 reuses its controls.
:::

## Asymmetry ≠ publication bias {.question}

::: question-card
[Your call]{.q-kicker}

[Our funnel is asymmetric. List **other reasons** than publication bias.]{.q-text}
:::

::: {.fragment .box .green style="width:80%;"}
-   **Heterogeneity**: small studies differ (other crops, pests, methods) — true small-study effects.
-   **Artefacts**: the variance of lnRR depends on the mean; extraction errors; pseudo-replication.
-   **Chance**: with few studies, funnels are often asymmetric.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Collect answers first. This is the key conceptual message of Dakis's lecture.
:::

## Testing for small-study effects: the classic way

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Egger's test** [@egger1997]: regress each effect size on its standard error. A slope ≠ 0 means small studies give different results.

Our pests: *p* = 0.00037.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.fragment .box .warn}
[Two problems]{.box-title}

1.  It treats our 382 comparisons as **independent** — they come from 28 studies.
2.  For lnRR, the SE is computed **from the means themselves** → an artificial link between effect and SE, even without any bias.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Let the room guess problem 1 (they saw non-independence at 14:00). Problem 2 is subtler: v(lnRR) = SD²/(n·mean²), so the effect and its SE share the means.
:::

## Testing for small-study effects: the multilevel way

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Add a precision measure as a **moderator** of the multilevel model [@nakagawa2022], based on **sample size only**:

$$\sqrt{1/n_T + 1/n_C}$$

```r
rma.mv(yi, vi,
       mods = ~ sqrt(1/n_t + 1/n_c),
       random = ~ 1 | study_id / es_id,
       test = "t", dfs = "contain",
       data = dat)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
| Precision measure | Slope *p* |
|---|---|
| SE (artefact-prone) | 0.018 |
| $\sqrt{1/n_T + 1/n_C}$ | **0.10** |
| same, cluster-robust (CR2) | 0.18 |

::: {.fragment .box .green}
With the recommended measure: **no robust evidence** of a small-study effect.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
~2 min. The SE-based test "finds" an effect that disappears with the sample-size-based measure. This multilevel Egger test is simply a meta-regression — the topic of the 16:15 session.
:::

## If there were bias, would the conclusion change?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
| Estimate | Pest abundance [95% CI] |
|---|---|
| Main model | -27% [-40; -11] |
| **PET**: effect of an infinitely large study | -43% [-61; -18] |
| **PEESE** | -36% [-50; -16] |
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
Rule [@stanley2014]: if the PET intercept is significant (here yes), report **PEESE**.

::: {.fragment .box .green}
Adjusted estimates are, if anything, **stronger**: the pest reduction is **not** an artefact of publication bias.
:::

::: {.small .muted}
With strong heterogeneity, PET-PEESE tends to **over-correct**: treat it as a sensitivity check, not as "the true effect". Alternative: **selection models** [@vevea1995; `selmodel()` in metafor], which model the probability of publication given the p-value.
:::
:::
:::

## Time-lag bias

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](slides_files/figure-revealjs/plot-timelag-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
Do early studies report stronger effects than later ones?

**Year as a moderator** in the multilevel model: slope = -0.0029 per year (*p* = 0.87).

::: {.fragment .box .green}
**No evidence** of a decline effect — with only 28 studies, the test has little power.
:::

::: {.small .muted}
Also possible: include year and SE together [@nakagawa2022].
:::
:::
:::

## Two classics to avoid (or to use with care)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.box .warn}
[Fail-safe N (Rosenthal)]{.box-title}
"How many null studies would make the result non-significant?"

Our data: **4,098,124** studies.

Meaningless: assumes missing studies have zero effect, ignores heterogeneity and dependence, estimates no bias. **Do not report it.**
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.box}
[Trim-and-fill]{.box-title}
Imputes "missing" studies to make the funnel symmetric.

Assumes asymmetry = publication bias, performs badly with heterogeneity, ignores dependence.\
→ at most a **sensitivity analysis** on study-level data, never "the corrected effect".
:::
:::
:::

::: {.source}
Source: @nakagawa2022; @ouedraogo2024.
:::

# Robustness {.section-divider background-image="../../theme/img/bg-keymessages.jpg"}

## Does one study drive the result?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](slides_files/figure-revealjs/plot-loo-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
**Leave-one-*study*-out**: refit the model 28 times, dropping one whole study each time.

-   Mean ranges from **-29%** to **-23%**
-   The CI never crosses 0

**Cook's distance** by study: largest = 0.32, no study stands out from the others.

::: {.fragment .box .green}
The conclusion does not depend on any single study.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
~3 min. Leave out STUDIES, not rows: rows of a study are not independent. cooks.distance(m, cluster = study_id) [@viechtbauer2010b].
:::

## A robustness table for your paper

| Analysis | Pest abundance | Conclusion changes? |
|---|---|---|
| Main multilevel model (28 studies) | **-27%** [-40; -11] | — |
| Only comparisons meeting all validity criteria† (13 studies; 130 comparisons not appraisable) | -27% [-39; -13]; validity as moderator *p* = 0.74 | No |
| Leave-one-study-out (range of means) | -29% to -23% | No |
| Small-study effect (sample-size based) | slope *p* = 0.10; PEESE -36% | No |
| Time-lag (year as moderator) | slope ≈ 0 (*p* = 0.87) | No (low power) |

[† Critical appraisal coded by @jones2021: enough sampling units in both groups, plots in their state long enough, intervention and comparator < 1.1 km apart. This is **internal validity** of each study (risk of bias, cf. CEE critical appraisal) — a different question from publication bias.]{.small .muted}

::: {.fragment .box .blue}
Also worth testing: another effect-size metric, the imputation of missing SDs, the correlation ρ assumed within studies. Report **all** sensitivity analyses — including those that change the result.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. This table is exactly what reviewers want. The validity subset uses the critical appraisal coded by the authors (this morning's session by Joseph).
:::

## Practical · 33 min + debrief

| Time | Task |
|------|------|
| 15:22 | Contour-enhanced **funnel plot** (code given: interpret) |
| 15:27 | Classic vs **multilevel Egger** (the lnRR trap); PET-PEESE |
| 15:37 | **Sensitivity**: leave-one-study-out, validity |
| 15:47 | *Your turn*: natural enemies — or the optional parts (time-lag, Cook, fail-safe N) |
| 15:55 | **Debrief** (all together) |

::: {.box .blue}
Open **`meta_analysis_course.Rproj`** (the course kit), then **`td_bias.R`**. Instructions and folded solutions: the practical web page.
:::

## Key messages {.key-messages background-image="../../theme/img/bg-keymessages.jpg"}

1.  Bias is best **prevented** by the search, not corrected by statistics.
2.  **Asymmetry ≠ publication bias**: read the direction, use contour-enhanced funnels.
3.  With several effect sizes per study, use **multilevel** tests — for lnRR with a **sample-size-based** precision; drop fail-safe N.
4.  Report a **robustness table**: leave-one-study-out, influence, study quality, analytical choices.

## In the online notebook {.dense}

Each point of this session developed further, with the same data, more pitfalls and exercises with solutions:

-   [Publication bias and sensitivity](https://literaturesynthesis.github.io/notebook/chapters/publication-bias.html)
-   [Data extraction and critical appraisal](https://literaturesynthesis.github.io/notebook/chapters/extraction-appraisal.html)
-   [Reading a meta-analysis critically](https://literaturesynthesis.github.io/notebook/chapters/critical-reading.html)

::: {.box .blue}
**literaturesynthesis.github.io/notebook**

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
